title: Sageuk Ink — Dancheong Title Card
description: A modern reinterpretation of Joseon dynasty drama opening titles: deep sumi-ink ground, a single horizontal dancheong band in vermillion and jade, and a heavy Myeongjo title set vertically with small Hanja episode notation.
philosophy: This template exists to bring the ceremonial gravity of Korean historical drama title sequences into presentation design. It rejects horizontal Latin-default typography and bright grounds in favor of vertical Myeongjo strokes on an ink-saturated canvas — the slide as calligraphic scroll, not document. The dancheong band is not ornament; it is structure, anchoring the composition the way a colophon anchors a classical painting. It is built for speakers who understand that deliberate restraint and authority are the same gesture.
goodFor: Opening title slides for Korean history, culture, or humanities lectures
Chapter and episode dividers in serialized long-form presentations
Film and drama pitch decks requiring a period-drama aesthetic
Single-statement hero slides where one idea commands the full canvas
avoidFor: Chart-heavy quarterly business reviews requiring data-dense layouts
Tech product launches that demand modern sans-serif grid systems
Decks with more than three lines of body copy per slide
Presentations relying on bright, high-chroma background palettes
author: harness

examples.promptCore: The slide evokes the opening title card of a Joseon period drama — solemn, ink-drenched, and ceremonially weighted. The dancheong band bisects the canvas with chromatic authority, its geometric pattern echoing palace woodwork rather than surface ornament. Vertical type descends like brushwork on a hanging scroll, breathing against the dark ground with deliberate, unhurried negative space. Avoid lateral document rhythm, Western-default centering, or any decorative lightness — this is gravitas rendered as pure composition.

examples.layoutNotes: Full-bleed ink ground with zero outer margin; the canvas reads edge-to-edge as a vertical scroll with no breathing border. A single horizontal dancheong band spans the full width at roughly one-third height from the bottom, functioning as structural horizon rather than decorative trim. The primary title text runs vertically in cols 7–10 of a 12-column grid, descending from the upper third of the canvas with generous negative space to its left. A compact Hanja or subtitle notation anchors the lower-left quadrant beneath the band at sharply reduced scale, establishing a two-register hierarchy without crowding.

examples.promptCore: The slide should evoke a page from a sageuk production manuscript — a single ink-saturated canvas where one idea carries full ceremonial weight, not a list of equal-priority items. The dancheong band is structural architecture, functioning like a seal or colophon that separates concept from attribution in classical East Asian calligraphy. Compositional rhythm is deliberately asymmetric: heavy textual presence on the right, wide breathing silence on the left — stillness as intention, not emptiness as accident. Avoid any visual gesture that reads as a Western document grid: no centered symmetry, no bullet cadence, no decorative flourishes divorced from structural purpose.

examples.layoutNotes: A 12-column grid with ~10% outer margins on all sides keeps the ink ground visible as negative space. The dancheong band runs as a full-width horizontal rule at roughly the lower-third break, functioning as a structural colophon line that separates the primary concept zone above from a narrow attribution or notation strip below. The primary content element — a short vertical text cluster of one to three concepts or a dominant pull-quote — is positioned in cols 7–11, deliberately off-center, with the left field held as intentional void. A small Hanja or episode notation sits bottom-left of the notation strip; no decorative header band at top, only a hairline full-bleed rule as a subtle frame.
